summary: Defines how to carry IPv6 packets over PPP links, including the IPv6 Control Protocol used to set up and configure IPv6 on a link. It describes how the two ends negotiate interface identifiers. It is a draft standard, a standards-track status.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5072 defines how two ends of a PPP link carry IPv6 packets and configure IPv6. They negotiate different 64-bit interface identifiers, which are used to form their link-local addresses.

subtitle: How PPP endpoints configure IPv6 and negotiate the interface identifiers used for link-local addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a defined way to run over point-to-point PPP links, including how the endpoints configure the protocol and choose distinct interface identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets use PPP Protocol value 0057, while IPV6CP negotiates a 64-bit interface identifier for each end and uses Protocol value 8057.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5072 obsoletes RFC 2472 and has been updated by RFC 8064. It also describes when duplicate address detection may be redundant.

today: RFC 5072 is a Draft Standard published in September 2007. It obsoletes RFC 2472 and has been updated by RFC 8064.

sections.title: PPP Setup and IPv6 Configuration
sections.content:
PPP carries network-layer datagrams over a point-to-point link. It first uses the Link Control Protocol (LCP) to establish and test the link. Network Control Protocols then configure the network-layer protocols that can use it.

This RFC defines the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP), the format for carrying IPv6 packets over PPP, and the formation of IPv6 link-local addresses. It replaces RFC 2472.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP first establishes its link, then configures the network protocols that will use it. IPV6CP performs the IPv6 configuration step.

sections.title: Sending IPv6 Datagrams
sections.content:
IPv6 packets can be sent only after PPP reaches the network-layer protocol phase and IPV6CP reaches the Opened state. Each PPP frame then carries exactly one IPv6 packet in its Information field. The Protocol field is hexadecimal 0057.

A PPP link that supports IPv6 must allow an Information field at least as large as the minimum link MTU required for IPv6. The maximum IPv6 packet length is the maximum length of that Information field.
sections.plainLanguage: After IPv6 setup completes, each PPP frame carries one IPv6 packet. The frame's protocol value identifies that packet as IPv6.

sections.title: The IPv6 Control Protocol
sections.content:
IPV6CP configures, enables and disables IPv6 at both ends of the link. It uses the same packet exchange mechanism as LCP, with Protocol value hexadecimal 8057. It uses codes 1 through 7 for configuration, termination and code-rejection messages.

IPV6CP packets that arrive before the network-layer protocol phase should be silently discarded. Implementations should allow authentication and link-quality checks to complete before timing out while waiting for a response.
sections.plainLanguage: IPV6CP uses a setup conversation to configure IPv6 on both endpoints. Messages that arrive before PPP is ready for network protocols are discarded.

sections.title: Negotiating Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
The Interface-Identifier option negotiates a unique 64-bit identifier for each end of the PPP link. Each Configure-Request must contain exactly one option, and the two endpoints must end with different non-zero identifiers.

An endpoint may derive its tentative identifier from an EUI-48 or EUI-64 identifier, use another source of uniqueness, or generate a random value. If the peers choose the same value, a Configure-Nak suggests a different one. If both values are zero, negotiation is rejected because the endpoints cannot establish a unique identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint negotiates a 64-bit identifier, and the two identifiers must differ. If they match, the peers suggest new values and continue negotiating.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses and Duplicate Detection
sections.content:
The negotiated identifier forms the local endpoint's IPv6 link-local address after the FE80:: prefix and 54 zero bits. The same identifier should not automatically be assumed for global addresses; a peer may generate other identifiers for those addresses.

Duplicate address detection on the link-local address is redundant when IPV6CP successfully negotiates the identifier. Detection on global addresses may also be redundant only when the router advertises prefixes exclusive to that PPP link and does not configure its own global address from them.
sections.plainLanguage: The negotiated identifier is used in the link-local address. Duplicate checks may be skipped only under the conditions the RFC specifies.

sections.title: Security and the Option Number
sections.content:
Without link security, global addresses formed from negotiated or generated identifiers raise the concerns described for IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration. The RFC lists traffic filters, peer authentication and encryption as suitable PPP security mechanisms, while noting that threats can remain.

IANA assigned value 1 to the Interface-Identifier option type.
sections.plainLanguage: Address configuration does not secure the PPP link. The RFC points to filtering, authentication and encryption as link protections, and registers the option type used for identifiers.
